fetched_contents.text: Amino acid composition in determination of collagen origin and assessment of physical factors effects Abstract The amino acid composition of collagen is a characteristic feature of this protein. Collagen, irrespective of its origin, contains 19 amino acids, including hydroxyproline which does not occur in other proteins. Its atypical amino acid composition is characterized by high content of proline and glycine, as well as the absence of cysteine. This paper shows the comparison of qualitative composition of amino acids of fish skin (FS) collagen, bovine Achilles tendon (BAT) collagen, and bone collagen. Results demonstrate that FS collagen as well as BAT collagen contains no cysteine and significantly different amount of hydroxyproline. In BAT collagen hydroxyproline content is 30% higher than hydroxyproline content of FS collagen. In bone collagen the amount of hydroxyproline is two times more than in FS collagen. Furthermore, it is shown that sensitivity to radiation of individual amino acids varies and depends on the absorbed dose of ionizing radiation. The changes observed in the amino acid composition become very intense for the doses of 500 kGy and 1000 kGy. Keywords Hydroxyproline ; Bone collagen ; Fish skin collagen ; Irradiation ; Polymer Introduction The knowledge of collagen chemistry involves primarily the knowledge of elementary composition, especially of amino acid composition, and the alignment of individual amino acids, e.g. the amino acid sequence in the protein molecule. The collagen triple helix is composed of three chains of procollagen interconnected by covalent bonds formed by concentrically located glycine. The spiral structure is formed mainly by alanine, phenylalanine, asparagine, glutamine, histidine, leucine, methionine and tyrosine. Due to the large size of the side chains, valine and isoleucine cannot participate in formation of a stable structure of the alpha-helix. The regular structure of the helix is disturbed by serine, threonine, proline, and hydroxyproline. The first two amino acids act so due to the additional hydrogen bonds formed by their hydroxyl groups [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. In case of proline, the nitrogen atom is embedded in a heterocyclic ring what eliminates the possibility of rotation around the carbon-nitrogen bond and prevents the formation of intramolecular hydrogen bonds. As the result of the proline presence, the chain may be inflected or even create loops. Protein content can be determined by the Kjeldahl method involving the mineralization of the test material with concentrated sulfuric (VI) acid, the alkalinization of the solution, and finally the distillation and titration of ammonia produced by the nitrogen connections contained in the protein. Thus, the analysis is composed of three stages: sample mineralization, steam distillation, and titration. In addition to the protein nitrogen bonds, ammonium ions and other compounds containing amino or imino groups may also be determined by this method. However, nitrates (V), nitrites (III), and nitrogen heterocyclic aromatic rings are not marked [6]. The Kjeldahl method is an indirect reference method which determines the content of nitrogen and then recalculates it into protein using corresponding conversion factors. In food products the determination applies to so-called total nitrogen (which includes protein nitrogen and nitrogen derived from the products of protein rebuilding) and nitrogen from other organic compounds. The average nitrogen content of proteins is approximately 16%, which is why the so-called crude protein conversion factor is 6.25 (100:16 = 6.25). Since the protein foods differ in qualitative and quantitative composition of proteins, the amount of nitrogen contained in them may also vary. For certain food products, different conversion factors are used, for example: egg protein—6.67 milk protein—6.38 meat protein—6.25 rye wheat, and oat protein—5.70. The multipliers are given next to the protein content, e.g. N = 6.38 for milk. Indirect methods may be used only when the test product contains no other nitrogen compounds or contains very few of them [7], [8]. Gamma irradiation from Cobalt 60 sources has been used to terminally sterilize bone allografts for many years. Gamma radiation adversely affects the mechanical and biological properties of bone allografts by degrading the collagen in bone matrix. Specifically, gamma rays split polypeptide chains. In wet specimens irradiation causes release of free radicals via radiolysis of water molecules that induces cross-linking reactions in collagen molecules [9]. Gamma irradiation is widely used as a mean of terminal sterilization for surgical implants and medical devices to ensure product safety. This technique offers advantages such as speed of processing and simplified handling of the material before and after sterilization [10], [11]. No toxic chemicals are introduced and conditions are relatively mild. Even though it is a convenient and cost method, it can have adverse effects on bioactive and biodegradable biomaterials. Gamma irradiation has been known to cleave chemical bonds of polymers including peptide bonds of proteins [12]. Damage to collagen by gamma irradiation includes molecular fragmentation via peptide chain scission [9]. The irradiation fragments collagen molecules leading to a loss of collagen network connectivity and therefore loss of toughness. Irradiation resulted in a 62% loss of work-to-fracture [9]. There was significantly less micro-damage formed during fracture propagation in the irradiated bone. Altogether, this new data strongly indicates that a large loss of overall collagen connectivity due to collagen fragmentation resulting from γ-irradiation sterilization leads to inferior cortical bone toughness [13]. S.Robins@rri.sari.ac.uk * PMID: 8855145 Abstract The collagen crosslinks, pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline, have been developed as urinary markers of bone resorption but, despite wide clinical application of the technique, comparatively little attention has been paid to the standardization of these compounds. In this study, pyridinoline and deoxypyridinoline have been purified from bone and converted completely to monochloride trihydrochloride salts. In addition to mass spectrometry and NMR spectroscopy, the purity of the isolated materials was assessed by microelemental analysis including the chloride counterions. These purified compounds were used to establish individual molar absorptivity values as primary standardization criteria for the two crosslinks. For pyridinoline in 0.1 mol/L HCl, epsilon at 295 nm was 5490 L mol(-1) cm(-1); in 50 mmol/L sodium phosphate, pH 7.5, epsilon at 325 nm was 5785. The corresponding values for deoxypyridinoline at acid and neutral pH were 5160 and 5290 L mol(-1) cm(-1). The availability of standardization criteria for the crosslinks will allow more meaningful comparisons of clinical data between different laboratories. Amino acid composition analysis (AACA) is a critical technique in biochemistry and the pharmaceutical industry, providing researchers with vital information regarding the structure, function, and purity of proteins and peptides. This analysis helps researchers assess the amino acid content of samples, ensuring that proteins and peptides meet rigorous quality standards. However, amino acid composition analysis is not a simple process. From sample preparation to complex quantitative measurements, this technique faces numerous challenges, such as incomplete hydrolysis, derivative side reactions, and sensitivity issues in trace-level analysis. This article aims to delve into the scientific principles and analytical methods of AACA while thoroughly exploring common challenges and their solutions in practical applications. Amino acid composition analysis is a quantitative technique used to accurately determine the amino acid content of protein or peptide samples, expressed as mole percentage or mass percentage. The analysis is based on the fundamental principle that proteins are made up of specific amino acids linked by peptide bonds, and the type and proportion of these amino acids determine the protein's molecular weight, isoelectric point, solubility, and other physicochemical properties. AACA works by hydrolyzing the sample to break the protein into individual free amino acids, followed by efficient separation and high-sensitivity detection techniques to identify and quantify these amino acids. Therefore, AACA provides crucial data for confirming protein identity, assessing purity, and understanding fundamental physicochemical properties. This technique is a foundational tool in protein characterization, quality control, and biochemical research. Fig. 1. Amino acid composition analysis (BOC Sciences Authorized). The Power of Quantitative Amino Acid Analysis The core value of amino acid composition analysis lies in its quantitative capability. This technique not only provides qualitative information (which amino acids are present in the sample) but, more importantly, offers precise quantitative data (the molar or mass content of each amino acid). By comparing the experimental amino acid composition to the theoretical values derived from protein or peptide sequences, researchers can: * Verify the theoretical sequence of a protein. * Assess the purity of the sample and detect any degradation or non-target proteins. * Evaluate the efficiency of recombinant protein expression and purification processes. * Provide reliable data support for subsequent structural biology, enzymology, or drug development studies. Quantitative analysis ensures scientific rigor and reproducibility, forming the basis of AACA's widespread application in biopharmaceutical and basic research fields. Applications in Biochemistry, Pharmaceuticals, and Food Science Amino acid composition analysis has widespread applications across various industries, including biochemistry, pharmaceuticals, and food science: * Applications in Biochemistry: Amino acid composition analysis is used for the characterization of proteins and peptides, studying protein-protein interactions, and understanding enzyme mechanisms. By determining the amino acid composition, researchers can gain insights into protein functions, predict their folding patterns, and analyze the impact of post-translational modifications. * Applications in Pharmaceuticals: Amino acid analysis plays a critical role in biopharmaceutical development and quality control, especially in the development of recombinant proteins and therapeutic peptides. It helps ensure the purity, identity, and potency of biologics, guaranteeing their safety and effectiveness in clinical applications. * Applications in Food Science: Amino acid composition analysis is used to evaluate the nutritional quality of foods, especially in protein-rich foods like meats, dairy products, and plant-based protein alternatives. This analysis helps determine the amino acid profile of foods, assess their nutritional value, and ensure they meet dietary requirements. By understanding the amino acid composition, industries can optimize production processes, ensure product safety, and enhance the effectiveness of their products. Why is Amino Acid Composition Analysis Critical for Research? AACA has become an indispensable tool in biopharmaceutical, biotechnology, and basic scientific research. It spans every critical phase, from gene cloning to drug commercialization, providing decision-making support for scientists. Verifying Protein Identity and Purity Verifying the identity of target proteins is essential during protein expression and purification. AACA can quickly confirm whether the target protein has been successfully expressed by comparing the measured amino acid composition with the theoretical values, while also assessing its purity. Strong progress has been achieved in the past two decades by 14C and stable isotopic laboratories in removing contamination from archaeological bones, but different pretreatment protocols have been proven to produce varying results. Here we compare three collagen extraction protocols used for palaeodietary studies and 14C dating, considering collagen yield, elemental and stable isotopic data, FTIR analysis, and 14C dates. Introduction Collagen extracted from archaeological bones and teeth is one of the most important biomolecules for radiocarbon (14C) dating and palaeodietary studies. Collagen Type I comprises ∼90% of the organic portion of the mammalian bone (∼22% dry weight of bone). A key concern of laboratories specialising in 14C dating or palaeodietary analysis of archaeological bone is the refinement of methods to extract and purify collagen for analysis. This is hampered by three key issues: * 1) The degradation of collagen through the rapid or gradual breakup of the peptide chains. This is strongly influenced by environmental conditions, with tropical or arid environments particularly detrimental to the preservation of proteins. The attack of fungi and bacteria can further alter the triple-helix sequence of mammalian collagen (Collins et al. 2002; Yu et al. 2014). In addition to hampering efforts to extract sufficient collagen for analysis, degradation can cause isotopic fractionation and therefore bias the interpretation of δ13C and δ15N values for dietary reconstruction (Masters 1987; Dobberstein et al. 2009). * 2) Contamination with exogenous carbonaceous contaminants can affect stable isotopic values and alter 14C dates if the contaminant is a different age to the sample (from modern to fossil carbon). Main challenges in interpreting amino acid analysis results

Contamination and non-collagen amino acids distort interpretation by introducing extraneous amino acid signals that can mask the true collagen profile. The evidence indicates that amino acid composition analysis is sensitive to contamination and derivative side reactions, and that sample preparation to complex quantitative measurements face numerous challenges such as incomplete hydrolysis, derivative side reactions, and sensitivity issues in trace-level analysis [N3-F3]. It also notes that the method is used to assess protein purity, detect degradation or non-target proteins, and verify theoretical sequence, implying that contamination can produce false signals that resemble collagen or alter the measured profile [N3-F3]. In the archaeological context, contamination with exogenous carbonaceous contaminants can affect stable isotopic values and alter 14C dates, while endogenous material such as bone lipids can significantly alter isotopic values if not removed [N5-F4]. Although these examples are not directly about amino acids, they show how contamination can interfere with biomolecular interpretation in the same class of sample.

Hydrolysis and sample preparation alter amino acid profiles by changing the extent to which amino acids are released and retained. Amino acid composition analysis works by hydrolyzing the sample to break proteins into free amino acids, then separating and detecting them [N3-F3]. The evidence also emphasizes that hydrolysis conditions, incomplete hydrolysis, and derivative side reactions are major challenges [N3-F3]. This matters because hydrolysis is necessary but imperfect: incomplete hydrolysis leaves some amino acids undetected, while side reactions can introduce artifacts or degrade some residues. In collagen studies, hydrolysis is also linked to the extraction and purification process, and different pretreatment protocols can produce varying results, including changes in yield, elemental and stable isotopic data, and collagen quality [N5-F4]. This means that preparation choices can distort the resulting amino acid profile even before analysis.

Post-depositional processes and diagenesis affect collagen integrity by degrading the collagen molecule and altering its composition over time. The archaeological evidence shows that collagen can degrade through the breakup of peptide chains, especially in tropical or arid environments, and that fungal or bacterial attack can alter the triple-helix sequence of mammalian collagen [N5-F4]. It also notes that degradation can cause isotopic fractionation and bias δ13C and δ15N values for dietary reconstruction [N5-F4]. In the collagen-specific context, irradiation studies show that gamma rays can split polypeptide chains, release free radicals, and induce cross-linking reactions in collagen molecules, leading to fragmentation and loss of collagen network connectivity [N1-F1]. This degradation changes not only the physical structure but also the amino acid composition, making preserved collagen easier to distinguish from degraded tissue. The evidence therefore supports the idea that diagenesis can produce a profile that is no longer representative of the original collagen.

Overall, the main interpretive challenges are contamination/artifacts, incomplete or inappropriate hydrolysis, and post-depositional degradation. These problems are not independent: contamination can mimic or obscure collagen-specific signals, hydrolysis conditions determine whether amino acids are fully released, and diagenesis changes the collagen molecule itself, altering the profile after the sample is extracted [N3-F3][N5-F4][N1-F1].

How amino acid analyses can assess collagen preservation

Amino acid analyses use a small set of collagen-specific and collagen-characteristic amino acids to infer preservation state. The evidence shows that collagen contains 19 amino acids, including hydroxyproline, which does not occur in other proteins [N1-F1]. It also states that glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline contribute to 57% of total amino acids in collagen, accounting for one-third of animal proteins [N1-R2]. A comparative study specifically compares amino acid compositions of collagens, paying special attention to hydroxyproline, proline, and glycine content [N1-R1]. In addition, hydroxyproline is described as a major amino acid in bone collagen and as a collagen signature amino acid whose determination is used to estimate collagen content [N6-R4]. These features make those amino acids useful markers: hydroxyproline is uniquely diagnostic, while glycine, proline, and other common collagen amino acids provide a broader compositional fingerprint [N1-F1][N1-R2][N6-R4].

Hydroxyproline and other collagen-specific amino acids distinguish preserved collagen from degraded tissue by serving as diagnostic signatures. Hydroxyproline is particularly useful because it does not occur in other proteins and is therefore a strong indicator of collagen presence [N1-F1]. The same source also explains that collagen’s atypical composition includes high content of proline and glycine and the absence of cysteine [N1-F1]. This means that when a sample is preserved, its amino acid profile should closely match these collagen-specific patterns. In contrast, degraded tissue may show altered amino acid proportions, lower hydroxyproline content, or appearance of non-collagen amino acids that are not normally present in collagen [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The evidence further supports this by showing that collagen can be distinguished from other proteins by its amino acid composition, and that the ratio of major collagen amino acids—3 glycine : 1 proline : 1 hydroxyproline—can be used to identify collagen-like material [N6-R1]. Thus, preserved collagen is characterized by a strong and expected collagen signature, while degradation weakens or distorts that signature.

Quantitative or qualitative thresholds suggest good versus poor collagen preservation, though the evidence provided does not give a single universal numerical cutoff. Instead, it emphasizes comparative and compositional thresholds. The comparative study compares the amino acid compositions of collagens and finds that bone collagen has a much higher hydroxyproline content than fish skin collagen [N1-F1]. It also shows that irradiation can reduce collagen integrity, with gamma rays splitting polypeptide chains and fragmenting collagen molecules [N1-F1]. This suggests that preservation is best when hydroxyproline and other collagen-specific amino acids remain intact and in expected proportions, and worst when those proportions are altered by degradation or fragmentation. The hydroxyproline dating literature also notes that hydroxyproline is used to estimate collagen content and that its determination is a well-known way to estimate collagen content [N6-R4]. Together, the evidence supports using hydroxyproline abundance, glycine/proline/hydroxyproline ratios, and the presence/absence of collagen-specific amino acids as qualitative and quantitative indicators of preservation: good preservation corresponds to a strong, intact collagen profile, while poor preservation corresponds to a weakened or altered profile [N1-F1][N1-R2][N6-R4].

Practical considerations for using amino acid analysis in bone preservation studies

Recommended controls and reference materials for validation are essential to ensure that the observed amino acid profile reflects true collagen rather than contamination or preparation artifacts. The evidence shows that amino acid composition analysis is used to verify the theoretical sequence of a protein, assess purity, and detect degradation or non-target proteins [N3-F3]. It also notes that the technique can be used to compare experimental amino acid composition to theoretical values derived from protein or peptide sequences [N3-F3]. For bone preservation studies, this means using reference collagen samples with a known, expected amino acid profile as controls. The evidence also supports using purified hydroxyproline and other validated reference materials, since hydroxyproline was purified from bone collagen and used as a standard for small-scale radiocarbon dating [N6-R3]. These controls help distinguish authentic collagen from contamination and confirm that the preparation process has not introduced artifacts.

When to combine amino acid data with other collagen assays depends on the goal of the study. The evidence indicates that amino acid composition analysis is used alongside other characterization methods, such as protein nitrogen determination by the Kjeldahl method and structural characterization techniques [N1-F1]. It also shows that collagen extraction protocols can produce varying results in terms of yield, elemental data, and stable isotopic data, and that ultrafiltration is used to improve purity [N5-F4]. For preservation studies, this suggests that amino acid data should be combined with other collagen assays when the aim is to confirm purity, identify degradation, or distinguish collagen from contaminants. The archaeological evidence also points to the value of complementary assays, such as FTIR analysis, 14C dating, and stable isotopic analysis, because collagen preservation is not only a biochemical issue but also a contamination and diagenetic one [N5-F4]. In short, amino acid analysis is best combined with other assays when validation is needed, when interpretation is ambiguous, or when the goal is to separate true preservation from experimental artifact [N3-F3][N5-F4].

How to report uncertainty and interpret ambiguous results should be done carefully, with transparency about the limitations of the method. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that amino acid composition analysis is sensitive to incomplete hydrolysis, derivative side reactions, and sensitivity issues in trace-level analysis [N3-F3]. It also notes that different pretreatment protocols can produce varying results and that contamination can affect isotopic values and 14C dates [N5-F4]. These points support reporting uncertainty by stating whether the sample was fully hydrolyzed, whether side reactions may have occurred, and whether contamination or diagenetic changes could affect the profile. Ambiguous results should be interpreted cautiously, recognizing that a weak or altered collagen signature may reflect degradation rather than absence of collagen, and that contamination can mimic preserved collagen [N3-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also supports using comparative thresholds, such as expected ratios and hydroxyproline content, to guide interpretation, but it does not provide a single fixed cutoff, so ambiguity should be resolved by multiple lines of evidence rather than one amino acid profile alone [N1-F1][N6-R4].

A result is reliable only when the sample context, preparation, and analytical conditions are favorable and well documented, and when the result is supported by comparative collagen profiles and appropriate controls [N5-F4][N8][N9].
